extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; readers interested in early American press development
extracted.subtask_description: Historical account of the development, role, and principles of newspapers and journalists in early United States history, with emphasis on press freedom, partisan practice, and frontier expansion of the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of the press (Hamilton's definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The liberty of the press ... consists in the right to publish with impunity truth with good motives for justifiable ends, though reflecting on the Government, Magistracy or individuals."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton's preparatory notes emphasize that publishing truthful statements with good motives and for justifiable ends must be protected even when they reflect on government or individuals; the allowance of this right is argued to be essential to the preservation of free government and its disallowance fatal. (Context: Croswell case; compared to Andrew Hamilton's 1735 Zenger defense.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth admissible in libel cases and jury as judge of law and facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The New York State legislature subsequently passed a statute "authorizing the truth to be admitted in evidence and the jury to be the judges of the law as well as of the facts in libel cases."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the Croswell argument and divided court, the lawmaking body changed procedure to permit truth as a defense and to empower juries to judge both law and facts — a practical legal standard for adjudicating alleged libels.

rubrics_metrics.name: State responsibility to punish slander balanced with useful freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Jefferson: "we deny that Congress have a right to control the freedom of the press, we have ever asserted the right of the States ... to do so. They have accordingly, all of them, made provisions for punishing slander, which those who have time and inclination, resort to for the vindication of their characters. In general, the State laws appear to have made the presses responsible for slander as far as is consistent with its useful freedom."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson's public stance recognizes limits: while protecting opinion, he accepts state power to punish slander so long as such laws remain consistent with the press's useful freedom. This sets a normative balance between free expression and legal responsibility for defamation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of opinion must not be invaded; honest actors have nothing to fear
rubrics_metrics.description: "The right of opinion shall suffer no invasion from me. Those who have acted well have nothing to fear ... those who have done ill, however, have nothing to hope, nor shall I fail to do justice lest it should be ascribed to that difference of opinion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson's principle for executive attitude toward press criticism: protect freedom of opinion while ensuring justice against wrongdoing. This is an ethical standard for public officials' response to critical journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers as necessary to popular government and publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: At Danville (1785) it was resolved that 'to insure unanimity ... and to give publicity to the proceedings of the convention, it is deemed essential to have a printing press.' Newspapers are presented as an essential symbol and instrument of popular government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly treats press/publicity as a civic necessity: newspapers give proceedings publicity, serve as a check on power, and are foundational to democratic development (especially in frontier/settlement contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Press should appeal to the reading public rather than legislative bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: "To the reading public they appealed; not to the House of Parliament, not to those alone who enjoyed the suffrage privilege ... but to the reading public."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic purpose in the period: shape public opinion directly, address the broader reading public, and thereby influence political development — a normative criterion for what journalism aims to do in a democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers as partisan organs and instruments of political struggle
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the narrative, newspapers function as Federalist or Republican organs (e.g., Pittsburgh Gazette as Federalist; many frontier papers started for political necessity), conducting attacks, counterattacks, and partisan mobilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historical norm: editors and papers often explicitly served political causes, used vigorous and sometimes 'vicious' attacks, and could provoke legal reprisals or personal violence. Evaluation of early papers must account for partisan function and political objectives (examples: Coleman, Callender, Croswell, Western World).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors/printers as active political actors and community leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Printer-editors frequently held political influence, obtained postmasterships, acted as local leaders, and were 'in demand' in pioneer communities; they were both 'mental feeders' and engaged in business/political life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical standard: in frontier settings the printer often doubled as postmaster and political agent; assessing a paper's role includes its editor's civic positions and federal recognition. Example: John Scull served as postmaster; the historical relation between post-office and printing office persisted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material and infrastructural requirements for sustaining newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: Early newspapers depended on paper supply, type, presses, transport (paper cost and carriage), and ultimately local paper-mills and type foundries (first paper-mill west of the Alleghanies 1793; type foundry not until 1820).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational criterion for producing a newspaper: secure material infrastructure (paper, type, presses) and distribution networks; frontier editors often had to improvise (e.g., borrowed 'twenty-seven quires of cartridge paper') and later established local mills/foundries to sustain publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic advocacy and legal defense of press freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Prominent lawyers and editors (e.g., Alexander Hamilton) argued legally for press protections; such advocacy could reshape laws (as Hamilton's Croswell argument influenced New York statute allowing truth in evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluating the press's role includes its legal and civic advocacy: strong journalism may require legal defense of publication rights and can effect statutory change. The example of Hamilton's 'greatest forensic effort' shows the press's dependence on effective legal argumentation to secure freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frontier/regional independence fosters distinct journalistic traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The feeling that the east was unfavorable to western development 'had a great influence in developing an independent western journalism' — the west produced vigorous, independent papers responding to local conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: regional context shapes journalistic style and purpose. Independent western journalism arose from practical grievances and local political needs; evaluating such papers must consider regional pressures, local interests, and how they differ from eastern models.
